body: “That’s always been the really long game, intentional pursuit that I’ve been on with the show,” says Denée Benton, the actor who portrays the enterprising secretary turned journalist turned novelist — and now, bride! — on HBO’s “The Gilded Age.” In an accurate reflection of the 19th century, Peggy has been handed some of the heaviest material on Julian Fellowes’ hit period drama. But Benton has also advocated for her character to partake in some of the lush fantasy that otherwise pervades the show. And starting with last season’s meet-cute with handsome doctor William Kirkland (Jordan Donica), Peggy did.

articles.title: Phoebe Bridgers’ Skeletal Transformation on ‘SNL’ Wasn’t Just a Startling Special Effect — It Emotionally Elevated One of the Best Pop Songs Ever Written About Death
articles.summary: On her first appearance as a solo artist on “Saturday Night Live” since 2021. Phoebe Bridgers didn’t break any guitars this time. But maybe some hearts. Or perhaps the impact was felt more as a chill down the spine.
body: If this were any halfway-standard “ SNL ” musical number, the visually shocking special might have seemed like a belated Halloween stunt. But “Still Standing” is an extraordinary piece of work, focused, as any serious fan well knows, on her father’s death. So at a key moment near the end of the solo acosutic performance, the abrupt transition gave an extra jolt of life, so to speak, to one of the best modern pop songs ever written about death and how we process it.

On the most mundane (but still fascinating level), there’s the question of how they pulled it off. It was a practical effect, and not a digital one. Bridgers was wearing UV-sensitive skull makeup under her other makeup for her entire time on “SNL,” including her preceding number. The changeover almost felt like a jump cut, but it was black lights making the hidden skull come alive.

It was spooky, but spooky with a point: Without trying to put too definite a meaning on it, it was as if Bridgers was having to go over to the other side, herself, to figure out how to grapple with a semi-estranged family member’s passing and legacy, since trying to get that right on this side of the veil is a pretty effed-up mess.
points: On her first appearance as a solo artist on “Saturday Night Live” since 2021.
Phoebe Bridgers didn’t break any guitars this time.

articles.title: Bill Pullman Starred In This '90s Neo-Noir Drama That Tried Suing The Oscars
articles.summary: Linda Fiorentino might've won an Oscar for her role opposite Bill Pullman in this '90s neo-noir flick, had its lawsuit against the Academy panned out.
body: Before we discuss John Dahl's "The Last Seduction" starring Linda Fiorentino and Bill Pullman, let's set the table. In the indispensable documentary "A Personal Journey With Martin Scorsese Through American Movies," the legendary director discusses the concept of artistic smuggling. The idea is that clever filmmakers can slip subversive themes past unsophisticated producers who are more focused on making a tidy profit than crafting a movie that means and says something.

Back in the B-movie heyday of the 1950s, this practice was common, particularly in genre pictures. Film noir offered a particularly fertile ground for such felonious messing around. Tales of compromised characters doing the wrong thing to get over or simply survive resonated in the wake of the Great Depression and World War II. People knew hard times and found cruel catharsis in watching folks trying, and typically failing, to game the system.
points: Linda Fiorentino might've won an Oscar for her role opposite Bill Pullman in this '90s neo-noir flick, had its lawsuit against the Academy panned out.

articles.title: Star Trek: Picard Started As A Pitch For An Underused Original Series Character
articles.summary: In its earliest incarnation, Star Trek: Picard was going to go in a very different direction by putting a familiar but underused character in the spotlight.
body: Over the course of its three-season run, "Star Trek: Picard" took viewers along for the final voyage of the legendary Starfleet captain played by the equally legendary Patrick Stewart. But while the series was heavily rooted in Picard's history, referenced storylines in "Star Trek: The Next Generation," and even spent its final season giving us the "TNG" crew getting back together for one last ride that viewers really wanted all along, the original idea for the show was apparently very different.

According to an interview with Trekcore, "Picard" co-creators Alex Kurtzman and Kristen Beyer started out with an idea that would've featured another character from the "Star Trek" universe that arguably deserved the spotlight even more than the famous captain: Nyota Uhura, the groundbreaking communications officer of the original "Enterprise," originally played by Nichelle Nichols.
points: In its earliest incarnation, Star Trek: Picard was going to go in a very different direction by putting a familiar but underused character in the spotlight.

articles.title: How Starship Troopers Author Robert A. Heinlein Really Felt About His Hollywood Experiences
articles.summary: Influential science fiction author Robert A. Heinlein dabbled in screenwriting for a time, and later revealed his feelings about his dalliance with Hollywood.
body: Robert A. Heinlein wasn't fond of working as a screenwriter in Hollywood, and he definitely hated working in TV.

The famed sci-fi author loved the movies, but was always more comfortable sticking to his preferred medium of the printed page. Heinlein was quoted in a 1994 issue of Cinefantastique Magazine saying that working on a Hollywood screenplay meant a great deal of stress, but also that seeing a completed movie he had worked on was a rewarding experience. Heinlein, however, was pretty negative about his experience working on 1960s TV. That, he recalls, was totally miserable.

Movie fans may know Robert A. Heinlein's name best for writing the 1959 novel that provided the source material for Paul Verhoeven's 1997 sci-fi war satire "Starship Troopers," a movie full of disturbing details. He was also behind the short story " '—All You Zombies—'," which was adapted into the wibby-wobbly time travel movie "Predestination." Sci-fi fans, however, know him as a giant of the genre, having written books like 1951's "The Puppet Masters," 1961's "Stranger in a Strange Land," and many others besides.

articles.title: Billy Idol Rebels, Phil Collins Gets Emotional and Rick Rubin Clones Invade the Rock Hall Induction Ceremony
articles.summary: Chris Rock roasted Diddy, Jack Black toasted Iron Maiden's no-show and Gwen Stefani sang with her teenage idol as the 2026 Rock & Roll Hall of Fame induction turned into a glorious, generation-scrambling mess.
body: Rick Rubin summed up the 2026 Rock & Roll Hall of Fame induction ceremony in one line: “You can’t kill rock ‘n’ roll.”
Fair enough, given how many people onstage Saturday night have spent the past half-century testing that theory.
And then there were the Red Hot Chili Peppers, who showed up dressed as Rubin.

Big white beards, balding white wigs, orange-tinted shades: the band turned themselves into a squad of Rubin clones and tore through “Give It Away,” the hit from Blood Sugar Sex Magik, the first album he made with them. Chad Smith’s bass drum carried a portrait of the man himself. It was the most gloriously ridiculous sight of the night, and proof that the Peppers can still act like the guys who once played shows in strategically placed socks.

articles.title: Ms. Marvel Star Iman Vellani Believes This Is The Perfect X-Men Story (And She's Right)
articles.summary: Ms. Marvel star Iman Vellani has highlighted one of the best X-Men comic stories of all time, which also had a major influence on the movies.
body: Whatever role Kamala Khan has to play in the Marvel Cinematic Universe, Marvel Studios needs to keep actress Iman Vellani on its payroll. A genuine comic book expert and enthusiast, Vellani is currently flexing her knowledge as co-host of Marvel's "Countdown to Avengers: Doomsday" podcast, running through all 15 films on the official "Doomsday" prep list. On the "X-Men" episode covering the original 2000s "X-Men" film trilogy, Vellani got into her love for the source material of "X2" — Chris Claremont and Brent Anderson's 1982 graphic novel, "X-Men: God Loves, Man Kills."

"If I had to recommend a single 'X-Men' comic that kind of encapsulates, like, it's the purest distillation of what these characters represent, it's 'God Loves, Man Kills,'" Vellani said, echoing common consensus among "X-Men" fans. The book's villain is Reverend William Stryker, a televangelist who believes mutants are demonic. When Stryker's "Purifiers" abduct Professor X in a plot for mutant genocide, the X-Men ally with Magneto against their common foe.
points: Ms. Marvel star Iman Vellani has highlighted one of the best X-Men comic stories of all time, which also had a major influence on the movies.
